old_title: Trump blames voters in Truth Social rant after stock market slump: Live updates
new_title: Trump axes chief of staff Susie Wiles as GOP points fingers at him over midterms

As Democrats continue to add to their "blue tsunami" of midterms wins, President Donald Trump has pointed the finger of blame at the opposition and at the American public for Thursday's stock market plunge.
The Nasdaq Composite dipped 5.52 percent while the S&P 500 dropped 4.36 percent and the Dow Jones went down 1,833.06 points in response to this week's resounding election results.
"The Stock Market suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election. Such a sad thing to watch!" Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Remember, it wasn't Republicans, it was Dumocrats."
In a follow-up post, he told the electorate: "You only have yourselves to blame!"
With votes still being counted in the Alaska and Mississippi Senate races and elsewhere, Democrats currently hold a 54 to 44 majority in the Senate and are projected to win 253 seats in the House to the GOP's 157.
The results come amid a civil war brewing within the Trump administration, with insiders scrambling to assign blame, the president reportedly sounding out advisors on the potential firing of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly on "resignation watch."
Hinojosa says data centers 'must benefit Texans'
Gina Hinojosa, the new governor-elect of Texas, has told CNN's Jake Tapper that data centers have a place in her state but only if they benefit the locals and are not foisted upon communities without proper laws and protections in place.
Trump's insistence on their necessity and indifference to the objections raised by rural voters may well have cost Republicans their support this week.
The president has already issued his first threat to Hinojosa, who will succeed Greg Abbott in January, over her border security.
Trump's DOJ looking at criminal investigation over Supreme Court abortion ruling leak
Federal prosecutors are actively conducting a criminal investigation into the source behind the 2022 leak of the Supreme Court's decision that overturned federal abortion rights.
Jasmine Fernandez reports.
The real winners of Tuesday night's midterms? Influencers live-streaming results
A successful midterms performance for Democrats highlighted an evolving battleground for news consumers, as digital livestreamers like left-leaning creator Hasan Piker drew audiences substantial enough to rival legacy media networks.
Here's more.
Truth Social: Trump vows to work with states that want to embrace AI
Here's the latest from the president on social media:
"As President, I am 100% in favor of Super Intelligence (SI), and will work with the many States in the U.S. that want to become RICH by having them. They are GOLD, and only foolish leadership will say 'NO' to the riches they bring!"
He has also clearly changed the channel on Fox:
"NEWSMAX: 'Trump is a Winner, and he's right on Iran!'"
Chuck Schumer: 'I am not the best bassoonist'
The veteran Democrat set to be the new Senate majority leader come January has brushed aside questions about his leadership of the party, albeit with a somewhat comic analogy comparing himself to an orchestra's conductor.
South Carolina senator-elect Annie Andrews, who beat Darline Graham on Tuesday, has already called for "generational change" in Congress amid concerns over the advanced age of some party stalwarts (Schumer is a mere boy at 75).
Top polling analyst pushes idea that Trump may just flat out 'quit' as president after disastrous midterms
Nate Silver, who correctly predicted that Democrats would regain control of both the House and Senate, has floated the idea that the president may just flat out "quit" as a result of his party's crippling defeats in the midterm elections.
Brendan Rascius has more.
Trump still backing Pete Hegseth as his seat gets warmer after midterm losses
Rumors continue to swirl around the defense secretary and his supposedly imminent exit from Trump's Cabinet but, for now, the president is continuing to support him publicly:
If he does stay on at the Pentagon, he could be the subject of an impeachment push by House Democrats, among whom there appears to be a clear appetite and a feeling that it stands a real chance of passing.
Here's Rachel Dobkin with the latest.
El-Sayed names his top three priorities for Democrats
The new Democratic senator for Michigan has been busy doing the media rounds since his triumph on Tuesday and yesterday laid out his top three priorities for his party in Congress, also issuing a timely warning against complacency.
El-Sayed remains a hot topic on Fox News, where Laura Ingraham appeared to agree with him about the war and former deputy FBI director Dan Bongino attacked him with an astonishing lack of self-awareness.
Judge blocks Trump's 250-foot DC arch within an hour of panel of allies approving plans
A federal judge has temporarily blocked Trump's administration from constructing a 250-foot "triumphal" arch that the president wants to use as a "top-grade military complex" to tower over Washington, D.C.
The late Thursday decision from District Judge Tanya Chutkan arrived within an hour of a federal planning commission filled with Trump's allies approving the plans, following several hours of public comments urging the panel to reject it.
Alex Woodward has the latest.
Trump teases 'big agreement' after meeting Putin envoy but not with Ukrainian officials
Speaking in the Oval Office Thursday - where he was, again, largely preoccupied with the decor - the president confirmed holding talks with Vladimir Putin's envoy Kirill Dmitriev, or, as he described him "head person of Russia" at the White House but admitted he did not meet with visiting Ukrainian officials.
"I can't tell you what I discussed," Trump said of his meeting with Dmitriev but did trail a "big agreement" forthcoming.
Here's more.

President Donald Trump has announced that chief of staff Susie Wiles is out and Stephen Miller is taking her place in the White House.
Wiles, who has been rumored to be leaving the Trump administration, becomes the highest-profile figure to lose her role after the Republican Party's disastrous midterm results. In her place, Miller will bring his hardline immigration reform.
The poor showing in the midterms has also left some Republicans questioning the future and looking for someone to blame.
Republican John Sununu lost in a Senate race and noted that voters said in 2024 Trump ran on a campaign of no new wars and draining the swamp. But, Trump went to war with Iran and there are allegations of his family benefiting from his time in office.
"And those two things, I think, caused people to say, 'You know, I just can't vote for a Republican while he's still in office,'" Sununu said.
The Republican's comments come as some others in the party worry about the 2028 electoral map, given the party lost races in key battleground states. Or ones that used to be near-locks such as Texas.
Republicans get a rare flip in the midterms
Republicans are getting a rare flip.
Democratic candidate Matt Dunlap has conceded the race for Maine's 2nd congressional district to former Gov. Paul LePage.
Not seeing a pathway to victory as the vote count moves to ranked-choice voting tabulation, Dunlap said in a statement: "This isn't the result we were hoping for, and I'm disappointed that we came short."
"Congratulations to Paul LePage, I wish him the best," Dunlap said. "I want to thank every volunteer who knocked doors, made calls, and made their voices heard."
Tucker Carlson says Trump era is over - and with it Fox News
Tucker Carlson declared the era of President Donald Trump - and Fox News - officially over, following the midterm elections which saw Democrats reclaim control of both the House and the Senate.
The former Trump ally and ex-Fox News host made the remarks on his podcast Wednesday, a day after Democrats romped to victory in a string of red states, ushering in an era of divided government.
Carlson called the election "the biggest blowout of our lifetimes," "a collective howl of pain," and a disaster on par with the sinking of the Lusitania.
Brendan Rascius reports...
Republican lawmaker says 'there should be some heads rolling' after midterm losses
Rep. Marlin Stutzman, an Indiana Republican, said the Trump administration should enact staffing changes as a result of the party's resounding defeat in the midterm elections.
"I think there should be some heads rolling from the White House right now," Stutzman told Newsmax on Thursday.
Democrats have now flipped at least 500 state legislative seats
Democrats have now flipped at least 500 state legislative seats, including picking up Democratic majorities in at least 12 chambers and breaking at least 11 GOP supermajorities.
"Donald Trump's failed legacy for Republicans now includes putting Democrats in their strongest position in the states in nearly two decades," according to Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee president Heather Williams.
"Statehouse elections will continue to have tremendous impacts on the future of our nation, and defending our new seats will be crucial to ensuring Democrats hold power over redistricting, voting rights, and protecting our elections," she added.
Trump proclaims the Oval Office a landmark - hoping nobody changes his gold design
Trump defends Pete Hegseth
During a Thursday Oval Office appearance, President Donald Trump defended Pete Hegseth.
"Pete Hegseth has done a fantastic job," the president said.
Some have called for Hegseth to lose his job in the aftermath of the midterm elections, where many voters cited displeasure with the Iran war and higher prices as reasons they voted Democrat.
